title: Chapter 66: Soft 4
content:
Chapter 66

They wound down the mountain path and slipped onto a hidden trail, leaving Cloud Recesses far behind. Once they were well clear of any territory frequented by the Lan disciples, Wei Wuxian suddenly whimpered, "Ow, ow... my stomach hurts."

Lan Wangji stopped immediately. "Rest. Change bandages."

"No need for all that," Wei Wuxian said. "Just help me get up on Little Apple and I'll be fine."

"Get up, then."

Wei Wuxian put on his most pitiful face. "I would, but hoisting myself up is way too much movement. I'm afraid I'll tear my wound open."

The wound had scabbed over ages ago; he was shamelessly playing the invalid. Lan Wangji paused, turned around, and looked at him. Without a word, he reached out—carefully avoiding the injured area—cupped Wei Wuxian by the waist, effortlessly scooped him up, and set him gently onto the donkey's back.

And so they carried on, one riding the donkey, the other walking alongside. Perched on Little Apple's back, Wei Wuxian grinned, his eyes crinkling into crescent moons.

"What?" Lan Wangji asked.

"Nothing!" Wei Wuxian chirped.

He felt the giddy, triumphant spark of a kid who had just gotten away with a petty crime.

Though most of his childhood was a hazy blur, one vivid memory remained etched in his mind.

A narrow path, a little spotted donkey, and three people. A man in black effortlessly hoisting a woman in white into the air, placing her onto the donkey's back, then lifting a tiny child high over his head to ride on his shoulders.

He had been that knee-high little kid. Perched on the man's shoulders, he had suddenly felt taller than the world, completely invincible. He’d tug at the man’s hair, knead his cheeks, kick his legs wildly, and babble nonsense. The woman in white swayed gently on the donkey's back, watching them with a soft smile. The man remained silent as ever, saying nothing, merely adjusting his grip to keep the boy sitting high and steady while holding the donkey's lead. Three people, squeezed onto a narrow trail, slowly meandering forward.

It was one of his few surviving memories.

Those were his parents.

"Lan Zhan," Wei Wuxian called out, "why don't you take the reins?"

"Why?"

Little Apple was smart enough to follow along on its own. Wei Wuxian chuckled, "Come on, indulge me. Take the lead."

Though still visibly baffled by Wei Wuxian's beaming smile, Lan Wangji complied, gathering Little Apple's reins into his hand.

Wei Wuxian muttered under his breath, "Yep... just missing a little one now."

"What?" Lan Wangji asked.

"Nothing!" Wei Wuxian gloated quietly. "Lan Zhan, you really are the best."

They were heading straight for Yiling—a trip into total uncertainty, with the odds stacked heavily against them. Yet Wei Wuxian couldn't muster an ounce of anxiety. Riding a little spotted donkey with Lan Wangji leading the way, his heart felt lighter than air, as if he were walking on clouds. He felt as though even if a horde of cultivation sects burst out from the bushes right now, they'd be nothing more than an annoying buzzkill. He even had the mind to admire the moonlit countryside, pulling his bamboo flute from his waist. Naturally, he brought it to his lips and played a melody.

The notes rose clear and bright into the night. Lan Wangji's footsteps faltered slightly. Suddenly, a lightbulb went off in Wei Wuxian’s head.

"Lan Zhan!" he gasped. "I've been meaning to ask you—back at Mount Muxi, deep inside the Xuanwu cave... what was the name of that song you sang to me?"

Lan Wangji looked back at him. "Why ask now?"

"Just tell me! What's it called? I think I finally figured out how you recognized me."

That night on Mount Dafan, the tune he had played purely on instinct was the very same melody Lan Wangji had softly hummed beside him while he was drifting in and out of a fever in that cave!

Lan Wangji kept his lips sealed. Wei Wuxian pressed, "Come on, out with it! What tune is it? Who wrote it?"

"I did."

Wei Wuxian blinked. "You composed it?!"

"Mm."

Wei Wuxian had originally assumed it was some top-secret Lan Clan hymn. Learning the truth sent a rush of shock and inexplicable joy through him. Shock for obvious reasons—but as for the joy, he couldn't quite put his finger on why it felt so sweet. He tested the waters: "If that's really how you knew it was me... does that mean you've never played it for anyone else?"

"Never."

Overjoyed, Wei Wuxian gave Little Apple an excited kick. The donkey let out a furious bray and reared up, threatening to throw him off, but Lan Wangji’s quick instincts kicked in as he yanked the reins tight. Wei Wuxian threw his arms around the donkey's neck, pleading, "Easy, easy! Don't mind him, Lan Zhan, he's just hot-tempered. Back to what we were saying—what's the song called?"

"What do you think?" Lan Wangji countered.

"What do you mean,what do I think? Does it have a name or not?" Wei Wuxian grumbled internally.Don't tell me Lan Zhan shares Jiang Cheng's atrocious naming taste? No way!He said aloud, "Are you asking for my input? Because I think we should call it..."

Eighty-something meticulously crafted name suggestions later—all flatly rejected by Lan Wangji—Wei Wuxian’s enthusiasm finally fizzled out.

To avoid running into cultivator search parties on the main roads, the two stuck to remote country paths. After a full day of traveling, Wei Wuxian was feeling tired and parched. Spotting a quiet farmhouse by the roadside, Lan Wangji brought Little Apple to a halt.

They knocked, but no one answered. A gentle push sent the door swinging open, revealing a small courtyard. In the center sat a handmade wooden table with a basket of half-peeled beans. Against the dirt wall stood a high stack of straw with a rake propped against it, and a brood of baby chicks scrambled around the yard, pecking at the dirt.

Noticing a pile of melons tucked in the corner, Wei Wuxian picked one up and said with deadpan gravity, "Since the host isn't home, Hanguang-jun, let's help ourselves."

Lan Wangji was reaching for his pouch to leave some silver on the table when footsteps echoed from outside the wall. Two people, approaching one after the other—the owners were back. The moment the sound registered, Wei Wuxian grabbed Lan Wangji and tackled him straight into the straw stack.

Only Lan Wangji’s unflappable composure kept him from making a sound as they went down. Yet he clearly had no idea why they were hiding. Even Wei Wuxian caught himself thinking,Wait, why are we hiding? Country folks aren't gonna recognize us. We could've just said we were here to buy food... Old habits die hard, I guess.

Still, tackling Lan Wangji had pinned the man flat against the soft straw. The slightly scandalous posture sparked a strange, wicked thrill in Wei Wuxian, so he decided not to get up at all.. Putting a finger to his lips with a solemn expression, he signaled for Lan Wangji to stay quiet, shamelessly staying sprawled on top of him under the pretense of necessity, his heart bubbling with an unspeakable, mischievous glee

The scraping of wooden stools echoed from the yard as the couple settled down at the table. A woman’s voice spoke up, "Er-gege, let me hold him."

Hearing the words "Second Brother," Lan Wangji visibly froze.

A man's voice replied, "Just peel the beans. I've got him." That was followed by the soft, sleepy mumblings of a young child.

A young family. The wife preparing dinner while the husband held their sleeping child.

Wei Wuxian gave Lan Wangji a cheeky wink, whispering, "What a coincidence. The master of this house is a 'Second Brother' too."

He drawled the words playfully, practically dripping with mischief. Lan Wangji shot him a heavy, warning look before turning his head away. Wei Wuxian’s heart did a little flutter. He leaned closer to Lan Wangji's ear and purred, "LanEr-gege~"

Lan Wangji’s breath hitched for a split second. When he looked back, his eyes burned with a stern warning.

Out in the yard, the wife giggled. "You don't even know how to hold him properly. If you wake him up, I'm the one who'll have to soothe him."

"He ran himself ragged today," the husband replied softly. "He won't wake up easily."

The snapping sound of peeling beans filled the air as the wife said, "Second Brother, you really need to discipline A-Bao. He's only four and already such a terror—what's he going to be like when he grows up? The neighbor's kid has run off crying so many times, swearing he'll never play with him again."

The husband chuckled. "And yet he comes right back every single time. Says he doesn't want to, but deep down, he's dying to play with him."

Wei Wuxian snorted, stifling a laugh. "LanEr-gege, what's your take on that? Do you agree?"

"Stop talking," Lan Wangji grunted.

At their quiet volume, ordinary people couldn't possibly overhear them. While the young couple chatted away about mundane family life, Wei Wuxian kept pressing his luck, cooing a dozen soft, sweet "LanEr-geges" right into Lan Wangji’s ear. Finally reaching his limit, Lan Wangji flipped them over in one swift motion.

The move was lightning-fast yet impossibly stable; the straw stack barely rustled, but Wei Wuxian now found himself pinned underneath.

Lan Wangji leaned down, his voice a low threat: "Say that one more time, and I'm silencing you."

Wei Wuxian reached a hand toward his face. Lan Wangji instantly grabbed his wrist. Wei Wuxian looked up with utmost seriousness. "Hanguang-jun... you've got straw on your forehead ribbon."

Lan Wangji slowly let go. Wei Wuxian plucked the tiny blade of straw, holding it up triumphantly. "See? Didn't lie to you."

Before he could gloat any further, the young wife spoke up again. "Still, you can't just let A-Bao pick on people like that."

Her husband replied casually, "Oh, let him be. Little boys are all like that—the more they like someone, the more they tease them. They just want that person's attention."

Wei Wuxian’s smile instantly froze.

Just then, the toddler seemed to wake up, babbling milkily. The couple rushed to soothe him until he drifted back to sleep. The woman whispered, "Second Brother, I'm telling you to keep a leash on A-Bao not just for that, but because things haven't been safe lately. Tell him not to wander off and to come home early every day."

"I know," the husband replied. "You talking about those old graves getting dug up near the village?"

"It's not just our village," she said, her voice dropping nervously. "I heard several ancestral tombs over in the city were hit, too. It's creepy. A-Bao needs to stay inside."

"Yeah," the husband agreed. "It'd be a nightmare if we ran into that Yiling Patriarch."

Wei Wuxian silently chewed on the irony.

The young woman shuddered softly. "I've heard stories about the Yiling Patriarch since I was a girl. I always thought 'Be good or the Yiling Patriarch will come eat you' was just something parents said to scare kids. Who knew he was real... and that he actually came back?"

"Tell me about it," her husband sighed. "As soon as I heard about graves being desecrated, I knew it had to be him. The whole city's talking about it."

Being permanently bound to the reputation of "grave-robbing" brought Wei Wuxian nothing but sheer helplessness. To be fair, hehaddone a lot of that in his past life. His most infamous feat was during the Sunshot Campaign, when he dug up the ancestral tombs of the Qishan Wen Clan, turning every last corpse into his personal undead army. Every Wen cultivator he killed was refined into a puppet and turned against their own kin. Back then, those deeds were hailed as heroic and glorious. But as time passed, people recalled them only with horror and disgust. Even Wei Wuxian himself, looking back, realized he had crossed a line. Combined with his identity being exposed just days ago, it was no wonder everyone blamed the Yiling Patriarch the moment tombs started getting dug up again.

A/N: In Chinese, "Er-gege" (Second Brother) can be a pet name for an older husband who is the second child in his family—which matches Lan Wangji's title as the second young master of the Lan Clan (Lan Er-gege).
